thread.title: Dow Loses 59 Points as Trade Talk Takes a Toll

author: Teresa Rivas
title: Dow Loses 59 Points as Trade Talk Takes a Toll
text:
Illustration: Getty Images By Teresa Rivas Sept. 10, 2018 5:17 p.m. ET New Week, New Gains. Last week’s losses are old news . Stocks built on early momentum to close higher on Monday, although the Dow didn’t join the party due to ongoing trade worries. Tesla (TSLA) certainly had a good day . In today’s After the Bell we…
• discuss why trade held the Dow back;
• but why investors aren’t too worried; and
• check in on Advanced Micro Devices ’ (AMD) big jump.
Tale as Old as Time
Stocks drove higher to start the week, even as trade led to minor losses for the Dow.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 59.47 points, or 0.23%, to 25,857.07. However, the S&P 500 climbed 5.45 points, or 0.19%, to 2877.13, and the Nasdaq Composite rose 21.62 points, or 0.27%, to 7924.16.
A decade after the financial crisis, billionaire investor Warren Buffett explains what was behind the 2008 mayhem, what we can do to limit the damage and opportunities missed last time. While a trade war has gone from horror to ho-hum for many investors, as a strong U.S. economy helps domestic markets rebuff worries in a way Chinese stocks have not, the threat still remains, and the numbers can still be scary. The president suggested last week that a third round of tariffs could encompass an additional $276 billion of Chinese goods on “short notice.” (The Dow, populated with big international firms and industrial, is often seen as more vulnerable the other indexes.)
As Glenmede ’s Jason Pride writes, “If enacted, this round would encompass all of China’s exports to the U.S. If all these tariffs were to be implemented, they could shave as much as 0.7% off annualized real gross domestic product via direct demand destruction.” Yikes.
Yet, as the Dow’s modest losses suggest, no one really expects things to go that far.
Trade remains a wildcard for sure, Nuveen ’s Robert Doll , writes, as “[e]very positive signal from the Trump administration seems to be followed by harsher rhetoric, making it very difficult to forecast the direction of trade issues.” He doesn’t expect much clarity in the near-term, and certainly not before mid-term elections, but his base case remains that trade turmoil won’t “derail the bull market or end economic expansion,” and ease a bit into 2019. “And as long as corporate earnings remain positive and the global economy expands, we see more reasons than not for stock prices to move higher over the coming year.”
So far so good on that front at least. We came off a great second-quarter earnings season, and while tech has taken its lumps recently – Amazon.com (AMZN) and Apple (AAPL) lost $100 billion in market cap in less than a week – that hasn’t sent the broader market into a spiral, as investors switch their bets to other sectors, such as health care.
“[P]rofits remain strong and the economy is in pretty good shape,” writes James Investment Research ’s Barry James . “Long-term momentum remains favorable as do our longer term indicators. We believe the market should be shifting gears and giving good opportunities for bargain securities.”
So for now, trade remains more of an annoyance than an apocalypse for U.S. investors. Don’t count on any resolution near term, but as far as Septembers go, this one hasn’t been too tough .
The Hot Stock
Advanced Micro Devices shot to the top of the S&P 500 on Monday, rebounding an nearing a 12-year high after last week’s selloff.
AMD gained $2.51, or 9.2%, to $29.89.
Tech in general rebounded today, including semiconductor stocks like AMD. In addition, AMD got a boost from Wells Fargo as analyst Aaron Rakers reiterated an Overweight rating on the shares raised his price target on the share to $34 from $20, writing that AMD will benefit from its ability to drive more than $2 billion per annum in server CPU revenue.
Newsletter Sign-up The shares are up 190.7% since the start of the year, and have gained 144% in the past 12 months.

The Biggest Loser
Brown Forman (BF.B) sank to the bottom of the index, giving up some ground after running up 3% last week.
Brown Forman lost $3.31, or 6.1%, to $50.71.
There wasn’t any new developments around the shares, but they had rallied a good deal during the short week last week, climbing more than 3%. On Friday, Jefferies ’ analyst Kevin Grundy initiated coverage on the stock with a Hold rating, citing the stock’s premium valuation from keeping him from a Buy rating.
The shares have lost 7.7% year to date, although they’ve risen 16.7% in the past 12 months.
